+
+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply every replacement of a _replace_table to s, in order. present is a
+    superset of the characters in s (a merge only adds its new token), so a
+    replacement whose pair has a character outside it cannot match and its
+    scan of s is skipped; the result is the same as replacing every pair.
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    add = present.add
+    for a, b, ps, c in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            n = len(s)
+            s = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(s) != n:
+                add(c)
+    return s

actions.reason: Skipping str.replace scans for pairs with characters known to be absent gave identical outputs, but encode_ir got 0.58% worse (ratio 1.0058). The C-level replaces are not where the time goes, and there is no budget left to profile further.

journal.text:
I tried to cut encode instruction count in minbpe by skipping str.replace scans for merge pairs whose characters are known to be absent from the text. The edits were in minbpe/basic.py (the replace table loop) and small matching changes in minbpe/regex.py.

One sandbox evaluation on encode_ir. Outputs were identical to the parent, but it was rejected for no improvement. encode_ir went from 425086578 to 427546720, ratio 1.0058, against a required 0.9900. train_ir also rose slightly, 369184757 to 369769863, ratio 1.0016. I gave up without submitting a candidate.

I now believe the C-level replace calls are not where encode time goes. The bookkeeping I added to decide which pairs to skip cost more than the scans it avoided. I never profiled, so I was guessing at the hotspot.

Next time, profile encode first and find the actual hot Python-level loop before editing anything. The chunk handling in regex.py and the per-chunk merge loop look like better targets than the replace calls.
